newsitem.title: GERMANY: German private banks say EU to probe public banks.
newsitem.headline: German private banks say EU to probe public banks.

text.p: Germany's private banks said on Tuesday they expected the European Commission would soon launch a formal investigation into alleged government subsidies paid to public sector banks.

The Federal Association of German Banks said that after years of fruitless talks aimed at ending an increasingly bitter dispute with the public banks, it was no longer prepared to seek an agreement at the national level.

"The scope for national talks has been used up and I expect the EU Commission to start an investigation shortly," Manfred Weber, managing director of the association, which represents private sector banks, told a news conference.
A probe would call into question Germany's giant public sector banking system, which is backed by state gurantees and therefore enjoys top credit ratings.

The dispute dates back to 1994 when the private banks filed a complaint with the Commission alleging billions of marks of state capital transferred to publicly-owned regional banks, or Landesbanken, since 1990 constituted a breach of EU subsidy rules.
The private banks see the transfer as distorting competition because it gave regional banks capital at a far lower price than that charged for funds in the private sector.

The German government, which is believed to be anxious to avoid a European Union investigation, last week applied to enshrine state protection for public banks in EU law as part of an amendment to the Maastricht Treaty.

While the private banks view the system of state guarantees for Landesbanken as unfair, their EU complaint refers only to 11 billion marks of capital transferred to the banks from state housing development agencies since 1990.
But the Commission is unlikely to act on that complaint before it sees how the German government's request for an amendment is received at an EU summit in Amsterdam in mid-June.
Weber said other EU nations and foreign banks saw the amendment as a problem.

"This isn't just a German problem, it's a European problem," Weber said, adding that the Landesbanken had international operations stretching well beyond their public brief of acting as clearing houses to domestic savings banks.
The association representing public banks said on Tuesday the Commission was unlikely to start an investigation before the end of June and it was unclear whether a probe would be launched at all.

"From what I have heard in talks with Commission representatives, this is a political issue and it's very open whether there will be an investigation," Henning Schoppmann, a director of the Federal Association of Public Banks, told Reuters.
The Commission's reluctance to intervene is well known as the issue is highly political, analysts said.

The Landesbanken are owned by their respective federal states and savings bank associations. They do not offer retail banking but compete with private banks in corporate finance, securities trading and issuing.
